narrative:
The model estimates you have a 12% chance of failing your final year. While this is a relatively low probability, it is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is your weekly study time. You currently spend only 5–10 hours studying each week, which is less than the typical amount reported by students who passed. This limited study time is the strongest reason the model leans toward a failing outcome. The second most important factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing, because students with a clean record tend to continue doing well. The third key factor is your reason for choosing this school—specifically that it was chosen because it is close to home. This reason is less common among students who ultimately pass and therefore pushes the prediction slightly toward failing.

To improve, you should focus on increasing your study time to at least 10 hours per week. Building stronger study habits now is the most direct way to raise your chances of passing and potentially avoid needing further remedial support.
